name: ABeta Amyloidosis, Iowa Type
aliases: Familial Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy, Iowa Type

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Diagnostic Criteria for Familial Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy

criteria.description: Identification of pathogenic mutation in the ABeta amyloid precursor protein gene (e.g., D23N mutation)
Demonstration of ABeta amyloid deposits in cerebral blood vessel walls on biopsy or autopsy
Presence of recurrent cerebral hemorrhages or progressive cognitive decline consistent with cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Positive family history of cerebral amyloid angiopathy or related neurological symptoms

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of pathogenic ABeta amyloid precursor protein mutation plus clinical features consistent with cerebral amyloid angiopathy and/or histopathological confirmation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing is critical for definitive diagnosis; brain biopsy is rarely performed due to invasiveness.

laboratory: CSF analysis typically normal or nonspecific
Exclusion of other causes of hemorrhage or dementia
imaging: Gradient echo or susceptibility-weighted imaging revealing microbleeds
Amyloid PET imaging demonstrating cerebral amyloid deposition
other: Histopathological confirmation of ABeta amyloid deposits in cerebral vessels
Family history supporting autosomal dominant inheritance

distinguishingFeatures: Lack of ABeta precursor protein gene mutation
Presence of E22Q mutation in amyloid precursor protein gene

redFlags: Recurrent lobar intracerebral hemorrhages in middle-aged adults
Rapidly progressive cognitive decline with vascular features
Positive family history of cerebral hemorrhages or dementia
references: Grabowski TJ, et al. Familial cerebral amyloid angiopathy, Iowa type: clinical, pathologic, and genetic features. Ann Neurol. 2001.
Revesz T, et al. Hereditary cerebral hemorrhage with amyloidosis. Brain Pathol. 2002.
Orphanet: ABeta amyloidosis, Iowa type. ORPHA:324708.
